title: Programming mindset & first program
subtitle: Programs, Python, print, comments, and problem-solving steps.
objectives: Describe a program as instructions executed in order.
Use print() to display text and values.
Plan a simple program before coding.
concepts: A sequence of instructions for a computer.
Python reads and executes instructions in your script.
Information displayed by a program; print() is commonly used.
Text beginning with # that Python ignores.
code:
print('Howdy, World!')
print(102)
print(2 + 3 * 4)
# Python ignores this comment
walkthrough: Each print() displays its argument.
Text needs quotes; numbers and expressions do not.
Multiplication happens before addition.
Comments explain code to human readers.
practice: Print your name, intended major, and 102 on separate lines.
Predict the output of print('A') and print(3+4).
Write comments outlining how to calculate rectangle area.
answers: Three print statements with quoted text.
Get length; get width; calculate area; display result.

title: Variables, assignment & arithmetic
subtitle: Names, assignment, sequential statements, arithmetic operators, and pseudocode.
concepts: A name associated with a value/object.
= assigns the right-side expression to the left-side name.
Statements normally execute from top to bottom.
code:
length = 8
width = 3
area = length * width
perimeter = 2 * (length + width)
print(area, perimeter)
x = 5
x = x + 2
print(x)
walkthrough: Variables store references to values.
area is calculated using current length and width.
x=x+2 means calculate the right side, then update x.
// is floor division, % remainder, ** exponent.
practice: Trace a=4; b=a+3; a=10; print(a,b).
Find 17//5 and 17%5.
Create distance=120 and time=3; calculate speed.

title: Types, input, output & strings
subtitle: Integers, floats, booleans, strings, conversions, input(), formatting, and string operations.
objectives: Concatenate, repeat, index, and slice strings.
concepts: Returns a string; convert with int() or float() when needed.
code:
name = input('Name: ')
credits = int(input('Credits: '))
print(f'Hello, {name}')
print(f'Credits: {credits}')
word = 'Python'
print(word[1], word[1:4], word * 2)
walkthrough: input() returns text even when the user types digits.
int() converts suitable numeric text.
f-strings put expressions inside braces.
Indexing starts at 0; a slice excludes its stop index.
practice: Identify types of 4, 4.0, '4', and False.
If s='Python', find s[1] and s[1:4].
Write input and calculation code for circle area.
answers: Convert radius to float, then area=math.pi*radius**2.

title: Boolean expressions & conditionals
subtitle: Comparisons, Boolean operators, if/elif/else, indentation, and nested decisions.
concepts: True when both operands are True.
True when at least one operand is True.
Select a code block based on conditions.
walkthrough: Python tests the first condition.
If false, it checks the next elif.
Only the first true branch executes in an if/elif chain.
Indentation defines each block.
practice: What prints when x=8 and x>10 is the condition?
Evaluate (4<5) and (8==8).
Write code that prints even if n%2==0 and odd otherwise.
answers: The else branch: small, if the two labels are large/small.

title: Problem solving & program design
subtitle: Understand a prompt, identify inputs/outputs, plan, pseudocode, test cases, implement.
objectives: Translate word problems into inputs, process, outputs.
concepts: An input with an expected result used to check correctness.
code:
# Average of three scores
# 1. Get scores
# 2. Add them
# 3. Divide by 3
# 4. Display
s1, s2, s3 = 80, 90, 100
average = (s1+s2+s3)/3
print(average)
walkthrough: Understand exactly what the prompt asks.
Identify inputs, output, and formula.
Outline the steps in plain language.
Translate each step into code.
Test with an easy case.
practice: Plan miles-to-kilometers conversion.
Give two test cases for rectangle area.
Write pseudocode for passing a threshold of 70.
answers: Input miles; multiply by 1.60934; display km.
Get score; if score>=70 print pass; else print not pass.

title: Loops: while & for
subtitle: Iteration, control variables, conditions, range, accumulators, nested loops, and loop errors.
objectives: Explain initialization, condition, body, and update.
Avoid infinite loops and off-by-one errors.
concepts: One execution of a loop body.
Repeats while its condition is True.
Iterates over items in a sequence or iterable.
A variable repeatedly updated to collect a total.
walkthrough: while checks the condition before each iteration.
Update count so the loop can eventually stop.
range(4) gives 0,1,2,3.
The accumulator adds each value to total.
practice: List values of range(2,7,2).
Trace n=1, doubling while n<10.
Write a loop summing integers 1 through 5.
answers: Trace each update and condition; values become 1,2,4,8,16, then condition fails.
total=0; for i in range(1,6): total+=i.

title: Lists & list processing
subtitle: Create lists, indexing, slicing, length, append, concatenation, iteration, and nested lists.
concepts: An ordered, mutable collection using square brackets.
Position; the first element is index 0.
A range such as values[1:4], including 1 but excluding 4.
Adds one item to the end of a list.
code:
grades = [87, 93, 75]
grades.append(100)
print(grades, len(grades))
print(grades[0], grades[1:3])
total = 0
for grade in grades:
    total += grade
print(total / len(grades))
walkthrough: append modifies the list.
len returns its number of elements.
Index 0 is the first element.
The loop visits each value and accumulates the sum.
practice: Append 50 to a list.
Find the maximum of a list using a loop, not max().
answers: Initialize best to the first value; loop and update best when a larger value appears.

title: Top-down design & dictionaries
subtitle: Decomposition, hierarchy, abstraction, key-value pairs, dictionary access, update, and iteration.
objectives: Update values and iterate over keys.
concepts: Start with the whole problem and divide it into smaller tasks.
A mutable mapping of keys to values.
An identifier used to retrieve a value.
Focus on a component's purpose without needing its internal details.
walkthrough: Dictionaries use curly braces and key:value pairs.
Access values with a key inside brackets.
Assigning an existing key updates it; a new key adds it.
A for loop can iterate through dictionary keys.
practice: Create a dictionary with name, year, and GPA.
Update GPA and add a major.
Name two subtasks for a study-session analyzer.
answers: Read session data; calculate summary; display results.

title: Functions: definition, calls & return
subtitle: Function headers, parameters, arguments, return values, tuples, and reusable code.
concepts: A named reusable block of code.
A name in the function definition.
A value passed when calling a function.
Ends a function and sends a result back.
code:
def rectangle_area(length, width):
    return length * width
area = rectangle_area(5, 3)
print(area)
def greet(name):
    print('Hello', name)
greet('Maya')
walkthrough: def introduces a function.
length and width are parameters.
The call supplies arguments 5 and 3.
return sends a result back.
Printing and returning are different.
practice: Write square(x) returning x*x.
Explain print(5) versus return 5.
Write a function returning the larger of two numbers.
answers: print displays; return passes a value back and exits the function.
Use a conditional and return the larger value.

title: Scope, parameters & mutable data
subtitle: Local/global scope, default arguments, tuples, unpacking, and list mutation.
concepts: A name created inside a function, normally usable only there.
A name defined at module level.
Used when a caller omits that parameter.
An object such as a list that can be changed in place.
walkthrough: Default values are used when arguments are omitted.
A tuple can package multiple returned values.
Unpacking assigns tuple elements to several names.
A function can mutate a list passed to it.
practice: What does f(3) return if def f(x,y=2): return x+y?
Write a function returning both min and max of a list.
Why can changing a list inside a function affect the original?
answers: Return a tuple containing smallest and largest.
Both names refer to the same mutable list object.

title: Debugging & error handling
subtitle: Syntax, runtime, logic errors, try/except, assertions, and systematic debugging.
objectives: Use error messages and test cases.
concepts: An error occurs while a program executes.
The program runs but produces the wrong result.
walkthrough: try contains code that may raise an exception.
except handles a particular exception type.
else executes if no exception occurs.
Logic bugs need tests and variable tracing.
practice: Classify missing colon, divide by zero, and wrong average divisor.
What exception does int('abc') raise?
Give test inputs for a nonnegative square-root function.

title: Files & string processing
subtitle: Opening files, reading, writing, paths, splitting text, and processing records.
concepts: Opens a file to retrieve data.
Opens a file for writing and may replace existing contents.
Separates text into a list using a delimiter or whitespace.
code:
with open('scores.txt', 'r') as infile:
    for line in infile:
        fields = line.strip().split(',')
        name = fields[0]
        score = float(fields[1])
        print(name, score)
walkthrough: with opens and automatically closes a file.
The loop processes each line.
strip removes surrounding whitespace/newline.
split(',') separates comma-delimited fields.
Convert numeric fields before calculations.
practice: Find the result of 'A,10,20'.split(',').
Why use strip before split?
Plan how to read numbers and compute their average.
answers: Read each line; convert; accumulate sum and count; divide.

title: Modules & engineering computation
subtitle: Imports, math functions, namespaces, units, and engineering calculations.
concepts: Names provided by a module or scope.
Using code to calculate, manipulate, or visualize engineering quantities.
code:
import math
radius = 4
area = math.pi * radius ** 2
print(area)
from math import sqrt
print(sqrt(81))
walkthrough: import math provides names through math.
math.pi is a module constant.
from math import sqrt imports one function name.
Check units and remember trig functions use radians.
practice: Calculate a 3-4-5 triangle hypotenuse with sqrt.
Compare import math and from math import sqrt.
Calculate sin(90 degrees) after converting degrees to radians.
answers: One imports the module namespace; the other imports sqrt directly.

title: Functions in program design & turtle
subtitle: Top-down/bottom-up design, hierarchy, abstraction, docstrings, and turtle graphics.
concepts: Start with the whole task and divide it into smaller subtasks.
Build small components and combine them.
Hide details behind a clear interface.
A string at the beginning of a function describing its purpose.
walkthrough: Give each function one clear responsibility.
main coordinates higher-level tasks.
Helper functions implement subtasks.
Turtle commands come from the turtle module.
practice: Design a hierarchy for reading data, computing statistics, and reporting.
Write a docstring for Celsius-to-Fahrenheit conversion.
Name a benefit of helper functions.
answers: main calls read_data, compute_stats, and report.
A short description of conversion and units.

title: Cumulative review & exam practice
subtitle: Mixed tracing, debugging, design, and code-writing across the course.
concepts: Follow execution and record changing values.
Run a solution against selected inputs.
Solve a new problem independently, not just recognize a pattern.
walkthrough: The function receives a list.
The loop accumulates the sum.
Divide by the number of elements.
print displays the returned result.
practice: Trace the example.
Add a check for an empty list.
Read three measurements, store them in a list, average them, and compare with a threshold.
answers: Check len(values)>0 before dividing; decide a behavior otherwise.
Plan input → list → average → conditional output.
